new_value: The Liberty opened in 1924 as a thousand-seat movie and vaudeville house and closed in 1982. Local volunteers restored it, and on July 11, 1987, it reopened with Rendez-vous des Cajuns, a Saturday night live show often likened to a Cajun Grand Ole Opry, developed with Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve. Folklorist Barry Jean Ancelet was emcee for twenty-four years and Ann Savoy booked the bands for the first fifteen, mixing Cajun groups, zydeco and Creole players and humorists. The show stopped in March 2020 and the theatre has been closed since. A local association is renovating it; as of 2026 it had not reopened.

new_value: Built in 1819 and 1820 for a Masonic lodge chartered by refugees from Saint-Domingue, this is the oldest Masonic temple in Louisiana. The lodge rented its ground floor for public events and held its rites and dances upstairs. In the early 1900s those dances featured the first jazz bands; Sidney Bechet played here as a boy, and riverboat captain Verne Streckfus came to scout Black musicians for his excursion steamers. Saved from demolition during urban renewal, the hall stands inside Louis Armstrong Park. The National Park Service gave up its lease in 2018. The city-owned building was renovated with state money in 2024, and early in 2025 it was still waiting for the city to choose a tenant.

new_value: Built in 1924 for the Grand United Order of Odd Fellows, the four-story building at 1335 North Boulevard held the Temple Theatre and, on its top floor, a ballroom called the Temple Roof Garden. With no comparable hall open to them, Black Baton Rougeans and students from Southern University danced here to touring bands; people interviewed for the building's National Register nomination recalled Fats Waller, Duke Ellington, Louis Armstrong and Cab Calloway. A 1938 advertisement called it the South's finest dancing hall. The Prince Hall Masons bought the building in 1948, and it was listed on the National Register in 1994. In December 2024 the city announced its conversion into 46 mixed-income apartments; it is no longer a dance hall.
